strengths: Well-motivated approach: Shifting contrastive learning from the cross-modal (image-text) domain entirely into the image token space is conceptually sound. It directly addresses the problem of limited negative samples in referring expression counting and avoids cross-modal representation misalignment.

The proposed modified supervised contrastive loss (L*sup), which restricts anchor selection strictly to the positive set to avoid pulling disparate negative tokens together, is logical and supported by ablations (Table 4).

Strong empirical results on REC-8K: C-REX improves notably over prior state-of-the-art GroundingREC (MAE drops from 6.50 to 5.06, RMSE from 19.79 to 17.53) and consistently outperforms the baseline across almost all attribute categories and count ranges.

Insightful analysis of detection-based counting: The paper provides useful empirical justification that re-purposing open-vocabulary detectors into centroid predictors is a primary driver of recent improvements in detection-based counting pipelines.
weaknesses: Potential risk of confirmation bias during positive mining: Selecting the top-N image tokens based on cosine similarity with masked RE tokens assumes the feature space is already sufficiently aligned. While supplementary notes indicate an ~80% accuracy in positive selection, early training dynamics and susceptibility to mislabeling under severe attribute confusion are not deeply explored.

Limited gains on class-agnostic counting benchmarks: On FSC-147, the improvement over the baseline is minor (10.01 vs 10.73 MAE), and on CARPK, C-REX performs worse than the simpler improved baseline (4.21 vs 3.80 MAE). While the authors explain why CAC benefits less, this dampens claims regarding general applicability beyond fine-grained referring expression counting.

Minor presentation issues and drafting errors: In Section 6 of the supplementary material, there are broken citations ('[? ? ? ]'). In Section 4.5.2, there is a typo ('choise' instead of 'choice'). On page 13, the text references 'the bottom sub-figure of Figure 6' when discussing failure cases, while Figure 7 appears to be the intended caption for that panel.

strengths: Clear motivation addressing key limitations of existing referring expression counting (REC) methods: moving from cross-modal (image-text) contrastive learning to intra-modal (image-space) supervised contrastive learning avoids cross-modal alignment instability and provides a much larger negative pool.

Strong empirical gains on the REC-8K benchmark: C-REX improves significantly over GroundingREC and the improved baseline across MAE (5.06 vs. 6.50) and RMSE (17.53 vs. 19.79), demonstrating clear benefits for disambiguating visually similar instances based on fine-grained expressions.

Well-structured ablation studies: The experiments effectively validate the proposed modifications to the supervised contrastive loss (only anchoring on positives in Eq. 4), the top-N selection strategy versus other heuristics (Table 5), and the components of the centroid-based detector baseline (Table 6).

Detailed qualitative analysis and breakdown across different attribute categories (e.g., action, location, orientation), providing useful insights into where intra-modal contrastive learning succeeds and where fine-grained counting fails.
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: The overall framework relies heavily on Grounding DINO, and adapting object detectors to centroid/point prediction has already been established in recent counting works (e.g., CountGD, GroundingREC). The core novelty is primarily the top-N pseudo-labeling combined with Supervised Contrastive Loss.

Mixed generalization beyond REC: While the method excels on REC-8K, its extension to standard class-agnostic counting (CAC) yields marginal improvements on FSC-147 (MAE 10.01 vs. 10.12 for GREC) and actually underperforms the authors' own baseline without the contrastive loss on CARPK (4.21 vs. 3.80 MAE). This weakens the claim regarding broad versatility across general counting tasks.

Heuristic reliance on the ground-truth count N during training: The positive sample set relies strictly on selecting the top-N image tokens based on masked-RE similarity. Although the authors show that ~80% of selected tokens are true positives, potential noise propagation and error dynamics under highly ambiguous attributes or images with zero true instances are not thoroughly examined.

Drafting oversights and broken references: The supplementary material contains unresolved citation place-holders (e.g., '[? ? ? ]' in Section 6), and the captioning/referencing of Figures 6 and 7 in Section 9 has discrepancies (referring to Figure 7 as 'the bottom sub-figure of Figure 6').

strengths: Strong empirical gains on Referring Expression Counting: On the REC-8K benchmark, C-REX significantly reduces test MAE from 6.50 (GroundingREC) to 5.06 and RMSE from 19.79 to 17.53.

Insightful baseline analysis: The observation that re-purposing open-vocabulary detectors (Grounding DINO) from bounding box prediction to point/centroid regression significantly boosts dense counting performance is practical and empirically validated (Table 6).

Targeted contrastive loss formulation: The proposed modification in Equation (4), which restricts anchor selection strictly to positive samples to prevent clustering heterogeneous negatives together, is intuitive and well-supported by ablation results (Table 4).

Detailed analysis and visualizations: The paper provides meaningful breakdown analyses across various object count ranges, attribute categories (action, orientation, location, etc.), and extensive qualitative examples including failure modes.
weaknesses: Unclear motivation for top-N pseudo-labeling given ground-truth point annotations: In REC-8K, ground-truth point annotations are provided for target objects. It is unclear why the authors select positive tokens using heuristic similarity ranking against masked text tokens ($I^+ = \text{argtop}_N(y_i)$) rather than using the ground-truth spatial points (or the Hungarian bipartite matching already native to DETR/Grounding DINO) to assign positive queries.

Ambiguity regarding 'Image-Space' contrastive representations: The paper repeatedly emphasizes operating 'entirely within the image space' to avoid vision-language misalignment. However, Grounding DINO object queries pass through cross-modality decoder layers that fuse text features. If $z_i$ are decoder query embeddings, they are already multimodal representations; if they are vision backbone tokens, the manuscript lacks technical clarity on how the 900 queries and prediction heads interact with them.

Mixed results on class-agnostic counting benchmarks: The proposed contrastive module does not generalize well across all tasks. On CARPK, C-REX (MAE 4.21, RMSE 6.12) underperforms the simple 'GDino improved' baseline (MAE 3.80, RMSE 5.16), and on FSC-147, the improvement over the baseline is minimal.

Methodological details and presentation oversights: Key implementation details are omitted, such as how the class token is masked in the text encoder (e.g., replaced by a `[MASK]` token, deleted, or zeroed out). Furthermore, there are noticeable formatting errors, including unresolved citations `[? ? ? ]` in Section 6 of the supplementary and an incorrect column header in Table 6 ('Number of Selections' instead of 'Method/Ablation').

strengths: Clear motivation: The paper identifies a well-reasoned limitation of prior referring expression counting (REC) methods—namely, that image-text contrastive learning suffers from a severe scarcity of negative textual prompts and cross-modal misalignment. Moving to intra-image visual token contrastive learning directly resolves the negative sample bottleneck by providing hundreds of negative visual tokens per scene.

Simplicity and model-agnostic plug-and-play design: C-REX requires no changes to underlying model architectures and can be seamlessly integrated into existing REC pipelines (GroundingREC, CAD-GD, GroundingDINO) by replacing or supplementing the contrastive objective.

Consistent and noticeable performance gains on REC: On the standard REC-8K benchmark across both Swin-T and Swin-B backbones, C-REX consistently improves MAE, RMSE, and F1 score across all three baseline architectures (e.g., test MAE improving from 6.50 to 4.91 for GroundingREC Swin-T, and from 5.90 to 4.38 for GroundingDINO Swin-T).

Thorough ablation and analysis: The paper includes thoughtful ablations validating the core design choices, such as contrasting image-space vs. image-text vs. joint objectives, bipartite matching vs. score-based token selection, and standard supervised contrastive loss vs. the proposed positive-anchor-only formulation.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is relatively incremental: Formulating contrastive learning on object/query embeddings matched via bipartite matching (Hungarian matching) is a standard technique in DETR-based detection and instance segmentation frameworks. Applying this specifically to visual tokens conditioned on referring expressions is a natural extension.

Inconsistent gains on certain configurations and tasks: On CAD-GD with the density-guided selection strategy (CAD-GD†, Swin-T), the validation MAE slightly worsens (4.65 to 4.70). Furthermore, under referring expression paraphrasing (Table 5a), CAD-GD + C-REX performs noticeably worse than the vanilla baseline (MAE 8.02 vs. 6.85).

Limited effectiveness on class-agnostic counting (FSC-147): While presented as a general approach, on the FSC-147 benchmark (Table 2), the gains are either marginal (GroundingDINO test MAE 10.73 to 10.04) or exhibit regression (GroundingREC test MAE degrades from 10.12 to 12.46).

Limited discussion of token resolution and high-density limits: While the paper notes that dense scenes consume more tokens as positives, an analysis of how performance scales with token count or grid resolution when counting very dense crowds (>500 instances) is lacking.

strengths: Clear problem motivation: The paper identifies a significant bottleneck in existing REC methods (such as GroundingREC and CAD-GD), which rely on image-text contrastive learning where negative samples are restricted to a tiny set of alternative textual expressions per image. Shifting to an intra-image token contrastive formulation effectively unlocks hundreds of visual negatives.

Sound and tailored loss formulation: Adapting the supervised contrastive objective (Eq. 2) to only use positive image tokens as anchors—avoiding the erroneous clustering of heterogeneous negative tokens (background, non-target objects)—is well-motivated, conceptually sound, and validated in ablations.

Comprehensive empirical verification: The proposed C-REX framework is evaluated across three architectures (GroundingREC, CAD-GD, and GroundingDINO) and two vision backbones (Swin-T and Swin-B), achieving solid and consistent improvements in MAE, RMSE, and F1 on REC-8K.

Thorough analysis and ablations: The manuscript provides informative ablations dissecting image-space vs. image-text contrastive learning, matching-based positive token selection strategies, robustness to linguistic paraphrase perturbations, and an interesting comparison against modern foundation VLMs (Molmo2-4B).
weaknesses: Mixed results on class-agnostic counting (FSC-147): In Table 2, while GroundingDINO and CAD-GD show slight gains, GroundingREC + C-REX degrades noticeably on the FSC-147 test set MAE (worsening from 10.12 to 12.46). This inconsistency is not adequately addressed or analyzed in Section 4.4.

Degradation on CAD-GD under paraphrasing: In Table 5a, evaluating on paraphrased REs causes CAD-GD + C-REX to perform significantly worse than baseline CAD-GD (MAE increases from 6.85 to 8.02, RMSE from 18.29 to 20.86). A deeper inquiry into why CAD-GD reacts negatively to paraphrases when trained with C-REX would strengthen the paper.

Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: Formulating dense contrastive objectives among transformer tokens matched via bipartite matching (Hungarian matching) is a well-established practice in object detection and instance segmentation; the novelty mainly lies in its empirical application and adaptation to REC.

Clarification needed on text influence: The text embedding still conditions the visual tokens through cross-modality decoder layers prior to computing the loss. The paper would benefit from clarifying how much text misalignment still propagates into these conditioned image tokens.

strengths: Clear motivation and problem formulation: The paper clearly identifies a major bottleneck in existing Referring Expression Counting (REC) methods—namely, relying on image-text contrastive learning where negative samples are scarce (typically fewer than 4 candidate expressions per image) and prone to cross-modal alignment errors. Shifting contrastive learning entirely to the visual token space provides an abundant pool of negative tokens within the same image.

Technically sound formulation: The adaptation of the supervised contrastive loss (Eq. 2) to only anchor on positive tokens is principled and well-reasoned, preventing unrelated background and distractor tokens in the negative set from being erroneously pulled together. The ablation study (Table 4b) convincingly confirms the necessity of this design choice.

Solid and consistent empirical gains: C-REX is evaluated across three distinct architectures (GroundingREC, CAD-GD, and GroundingDINO) and two vision backbones (Swin-T and Swin-B) on REC-8K. It achieves solid performance improvements across MAE, RMSE, and F1 score, demonstrating its versatility as a drop-in component.

Comprehensive ablations and analysis: The paper includes insightful ablation studies comparing image-space vs. image-text contrastive objectives (Table 3), token selection mechanisms (Table 4a), robustness under linguistic paraphrasing (Table 5a), and comparison against open-source foundation VLMs like Molmo2-4B (Table 5b).
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: While the empirical execution and application to REC are solid, the conceptual novelty of applying token-level supervised contrastive learning based on bipartite matching assignments is relatively modest, as similar patch/token contrastive strategies have been widely explored in detection, re-identification, and dense visual representation learning.

Mixed or minor gains in secondary settings: On the FSC-147 class-agnostic counting benchmark (Table 2), the improvements are marginal or occasionally negative (e.g., GroundingREC test MAE degrades from 10.12 to 12.46). Additionally, under paraphrased referring expressions (Table 5a), CAD-GD degrades when equipped with C-REX (MAE increases from 6.85 to 8.02), indicating that purely image-space supervision may occasionally decrease tolerance to prompt phrasing variations.

Lack of analysis on bipartite matching stability: Because positive tokens are assigned on-the-fly via bipartite matching during training, early training iterations could produce unstable positive/negative assignments. An analysis of training stability, convergence behavior, or sensitivity to the contrastive temperature parameter $\tau$ would provide deeper technical insight.
